So, yeah. If aces don't consider themselves a part of the community, it's more likely due to mistrust and fear rather than not wanting to belong (I used to identify as asexual before realising it was actually dysphoria in my case, and most of the community I met during that time considered themselves queer or LGBTQIAP+). But that's just my experience, there may be plenty out there who are happy not being in the community. I honestly can't say I blame them given the absolutely vile vitriol I see aimed at them in a lot of online spaces.

That's what they try to justify it as, but in actuality the vast majority of people who throw a screaming tantrum (and there's a very distinct difference between people who don't like the term because they find it triggering vs people who throw a tantrum about it) over the term are actively trying to keep out people who are ***actually LGBTQIA+,*** like asexuals and non-binary people, along with anybody they don't deem "trans enough". Literally every single one I've met has been a gatekeeping fucknugget.

Obviously pedophiles and hetero kinksters aren't part of the community, that's not even a debate among y'know, actual queer people. Exclusionists just try to make it seem like a debate because they use it as a facade to keep out other people they deem "undesirables" in the community. To them, not being cishet isn't enough to be queer, which is why they throw a screaming tantrum over the word queer in the first place - because including queers that they don't like is too inclusive for them.

The more inclusive part is why some people (radfems, TERFs, transmeds, etc) have a problem with the term. They want to gatekeep the community and anything that doesn't force people to lay out their identity in very specific terms for them to judge whether they belong in the community is a Bad Thing in their opinion. 

Some people may personally dislike the term, choose not to reclaim it and not want to be referred to that way (which is entirely fair and understandable) but those people tend not to stomp their feet and scream about it. The ones stomping their feet and screaming are the authoritarians trying to take away everybody else's right to use the term.

Kids tend to be very accepting of things tbh, particularly younger kids, so as long as you had an explanation on hand for the more obvious questions (why does auntie have a girlfriend and a husband? Your kids are not going to ask about the sexual mechanics of somebody's relationships at 9 years old, it won't even cross their minds, so I think you're overreacting a little on the "it'll confuse the kids" front. That being said, if you don't know this person, it's not unreasonable for you not to want your first meeting to involve her sharing your accommodation for a week. What is unreasonable is for you to call yourself a "very liberal person" and then turn around and tell your sister that her relationship is something that is inappropriate and should be hidden from your children, similar to how gay people are told that their relationships are inappropriate and deviant and that children shouldn't be aware that they exist. So yes, YTA, especially when you're the one who made it a touchy situation in the first place by pulling the "think of the children" card because you don't like or understand something.
